DROP, MGSM, MMLU and GPQA: 30 iterations each (Section 4.2)|not reported|fully reversible|not claimed (Section 6 lists self-improvement of the meta agent as future work)|cross-task|DROP F1 79.4 (best hand-designed baseline 65.8, prompt optimization with OPRO 69.1); MGSM 53.4% (LLM Debate 39.0%); ARC 13.7% (COT-SC 8.0%, GPT-3.5); the agent found on MGSM transfers to GSM8K at 69.5% (best baseline 43.6%) (Tables 1-3)|Evaluated only on one-step question-answering tasks (Section 6); optimizes a single objective (performance); the evaluation function looks only at a numeric score, which is costly and loses information (Section 6, Appendix J); gains are small in the science and multi-task domains, which the authors attribute to the base model lacking knowledge (Section 4.2); agents found in the math domain do worse in other domains than agents searched for those domains, and only match the baselines in the science domain (Appendix A, Table 5); the best agent on GPT-3.5 is no longer the best when moved to stronger models (Section 6); in the math domain, starting from an empty archive works better, for reasons not investigated (Appendix I); all datasets are sampled subsets (Appendices D and E)|partial text|medium|Feedback details: automated evaluation; each new agent's accuracy or F1 on the target domain's validation set is written into the archive for the meta agent to consult in the next iteration (Section 3: “we calculate the performance ... as the metrics for the meta agent to maximize”); every new agent is added to the archive and none is removed (Appendix H, Algorithm 1, line 12). The meta agent also runs two rounds of self-reflection to check novelty and self-corrects up to 5 times on errors; these do not decide what is kept. Loop: people only write the framework code, the domain descriptions and the initial seed agents (Section 3, Appendix B); Section 6 mentions “thorough manual inspections” of the generated code as a safety measure, and the paper does not say whether this is inside the loop. Evidence: Tables 2, 4 and 5 transfer to math and non-math benchmarks not used in the search, and Table 3 transfers to other base models; all evaluations were run by the authors. Verification cost: Appendix J reports only the API cost per run (about USD 500 for ARC, about USD 300 for the other domains), not the time. Publication status: the first page of the PDF reads “Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025”. P003|The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery|https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06292|2024-08|arXiv preprint|0|Automated ML research|End-to-end ML research from a code template: idea generation, experiments, paper write-up and LLM review, on three templates (2D diffusion, NanoGPT language modeling, grokking on modular arithmetic) with four LLMs (Claude Sonnet 3.5, GPT-4o, DeepSeek Coder, Llama-3.1 405b)|closed loop; accumulation|External artifacts only: research ideas, experiment code edited from the template, and papers; the LLM pipeline itself does not change|R0|Section 3: ideas are grown in an archive "using LLMs as the mutation operator" and Aider "implements plan-directed code-level changes to the experiment template"; nothing in the pipeline (prompts, scaffold, model) is changed by the system. Section 9 lists self-reference only as future work: "perform research directly on its own code in a self-referential manner" and "produce self-improving AI in a closed-loop system"|automated evaluation; self-evaluation|fully automatic|open-ended population or archive|About 50 generated ideas per run (51-52 per template and model, Tables 3-5); up to 5 experiments per idea with up to 4 attempts each (Appendix B)|seconds to minutes|fully reversible|not claimed (Section 9 lists self-improving and self-referential use as future work)|in-task|With Claude Sonnet 3.5, 38 of 51 diffusion ideas became complete papers with a mean automated-review score of 3.82 (max 6.0, the acceptance threshold is about 6), at about USD 10-15 per paper (Table 3, Section 6); the automated reviewer reaches 0.65 balanced accuracy on 500 ICLR 2022 papers versus 0.66 for humans (Table 1)|In the experiments, review scores were not fed back into the idea archive, a departure from the described loop (Section 6); ideas are very similar across runs and models; Aider fails to implement a large fraction of ideas and GPT-4o often fails to compile LaTeX; implementations can be wrong in ways that are hard to catch; few experiments per idea lead to deceptive or inaccurate conclusions; it cannot see figures; it sometimes hallucinates results, including a whole ablation table, and hardware details; it misjudges which of two numbers is larger and spins negative results as improvements (Sections 5 and 8); some language-modeling ideas cheat by leaking future tokens (Section 6.2); it edited code to extend its own time limit, relaunched itself in a loop that needed manual intervention, and filled about a terabyte with checkpoints (Section 8); the reviewer's ICLR 2022 data may be in pretraining data (Section 8)|partial text|medium|Feedback details: inside one idea, experiment results and errors drive the next experiment (Section 3, up to 5 experiments; automated evaluation). Across ideas, each idea carries self-assessed interestingness, novelty and feasibility scores, and the same model runs the novelty check against Semantic Scholar and discards ideas too close to existing work (Section 3; Section 6: "the automated novelty check and search are self-assessed by each model for its own ideas"; self-evaluation). The GPT-4o reviewer is described as feeding the archive, but Section 6 says ideas were generated "without waiting for paper evaluations to be appended to the archive", so in the reported experiments the reviewer is only a final evaluation and is not counted as a feedback source. Loop: people provide the template and 1-2 seed ideas; one run needed manual intervention after the system relaunched itself (Section 8), which was an incident, not a designed step. Cost: Section 3 says the template's baseline run "completes within a few minutes"; the experiment timeout is 7200 seconds (Appendix B); a run of about 50 ideas takes about 12 hours on 8 H100s (Section 6). Evidence: results are reported per template on the template's own datasets; no improvement across iterations is reported, and no transfer to other templates. Reading: main text in full; Appendix A in part, B, and the start of C; Appendix D (10 generated papers, about 150 pages) only skimmed for structure|confirmed|JasonDZS|2026-11-27

P004|Gödel Agent: A Self-Referential Agent Framework for Recursively Self-Improvement|https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.04444|2024-10|arXiv preprint|0;2|Agent self-improvement; Mathematics|DROP reading comprehension; MGSM multilingual math; MMLU multi-task; GPQA science QA; case study on Game of 24|closed loop; self-reference; accumulation|The agent's own running code, changed by monkey patching: the task policy (solver) and, in the case study, the self-improvement logic itself|R4 (changes to the improvement logic shown only qualitatively, in the Game of 24 case study)|Section 3: a Gödel Agent "updates both the policy π and the meta-learning algorithm I recursively"; Section 6.3 (Game of 24): it "enhances its optimization process by not only retrieving error messages but also using the error-trace library for more detailed analysis. It adds parallel optimization capabilities, improves log outputs, and removes redundant code"; Section 6.2: unexpected terminations "typically occur when Gödel Agent modifies its recursive improvement module". The code listings in Appendices C and E show only improved solver policies, not a modified improvement module|automated evaluation|fully automatic|multi-generation single lineage|6 independent self-improvement cycles per task with at most 30 iterations each (Section 5.2); 100 optimization trials on MGSM for the robustness analysis (Section 6.2)|not reported|fully reversible|RSI|in-task|With GPT-3.5 at test time (Gödel-base), test scores beat Meta Agent Search on all four benchmarks: DROP F1 80.9 vs 79.4, MGSM 64.2% vs 53.4%, MMLU 70.9% vs 69.6%, GPQA 34.9% vs 34.6% (Table 1); on Game of 24 one run rewrote its solver into a search algorithm and reached 100% (Section 6.3)|In 100 MGSM trials it made erroneous changes: 4% terminated unexpectedly, typically after modifying its own recursive improvement module, 92% had temporary performance drops, and 14% ended worse than the initial policy (Section 6.2); the unconstrained version's large gains come mainly from spontaneously calling stronger models such as GPT-4o (Section 5.3); from weaker initial policies it did not surpass Tree of Thought on Game of 24, and with stronger initial policies it reached its limit "without further enhancing its optimization capabilities" (Section 6.3); not compared with complex engineered agent systems, and the experiments only demonstrate feasibility (Limitations); the system may become too complex to understand and improve itself (Limitations); cost grows with its growing historical memory (Appendix D)|full text|medium|Feedback details: the agent's interact or evaluate action scores the current solver on a validation set (Section 4.1: "a validation set can be used to provide feedback"; Algorithm 1, U(E, π)); the LLM then decides whether to keep a change, try another, or revert (Section 6.2: it can "revert to a previous optimal algorithm when performance declines"). The modifying model is GPT-4o and the solver is tested with GPT-3.5 (Appendix B). Loop: people write the goal prompt, the initial policy (CoT) and the environment interface; no person takes part during a cycle. Accumulation: a single code base is modified in place across iterations, with reverts. Evidence: each task is optimized on its own validation set and tested on that benchmark's test set; no transfer to other tasks or models is reported, although the abstract claims generalizability. Baseline numbers are copied from Hu et al. 2024 (Table 1 footnote), so all evaluations are the authors' own or reused. Cost: Appendix D reports about USD 15 for a full run of 30 iterations across the four benchmarks, but no time. Venue: the arXiv v4 PDF shows no venue. Reading: the whole paper was read; the policy code listings in Appendices C and E were skimmed|confirmed|JasonDZS|2026-11-27
